teile.einleitung: The cheetah is the fastest land animal in the world. At up to 100 kilometres per hour it chases after gazelles in the savannahs of Africa. But its sprint is so exhausting that afterwards it first has to catch its breath.
wichtigste: The cheetah is the fastest land animal in the world and reaches up to 100 km/h.
A full-grown cheetah weighs about 40 to 60 kilograms.
It lives mainly in Africa, with a small remnant group in Iran as well.
Black tear stripes on its face are its trademark.
It creeps up on its prey and then sprints off.
Only the mother looks after the young.
The cheetah is considered vulnerable.

abschnitte.text: The cheetah is slim and long-legged, almost like a greyhound among the cats. It weighs about 40 to 60 kilograms. Its yellowish coat bears small, round black spots, and the belly is pale or white. From the eye to the mouth run two black **tear stripes**. It is suspected that, as with athletes, they reduce glare from the sun.

The cheetah can run up to 100 kilometres per hour, but only for a short time. Its flexible spine stretches and bends like a spring with every bound. Particularly large nostrils and a large lung help it to take in plenty of air as it runs. It needs its long **tail** for steering and keeping its balance in tight turns. It can retract its **claws** only partly, and they give it grip like the spikes on running shoes.

The cheetah mostly hunts by day, often in the morning or late afternoon. It creeps up and then sprints off, and a sprint usually lasts less than a minute. Its prey is mainly smaller antelopes such as the Thomson's gazelle or impalas. It brings them down with a blow of its paw and holds on to their throat. After the sprint it is often too exhausted to fight, so it sometimes loses its prey to lions or hyenas.

After a pregnancy of about three months, the female usually gives birth to three to five young. Only the mother looks after the young, and she raises them for one and a half to two years. Small cheetah cubs have long, grey fur on their backs that camouflages them in the grass. **Lions and hyenas** are particularly dangerous for them, and many cubs do not survive the first months. Male siblings often stay together as a group and hunt together.

In the past, cheetahs lived in large parts of Africa and Asia as far as India. Today there are only about 7,000 animals in the wild (an estimate from around 2020), almost all in Africa. In Iran only a tiny group of the **Asiatic cheetah** survives. The cheetah is threatened by the loss of its habitat, conflicts with farmers and the illegal trade in young animals. On the Red List it is considered vulnerable.

begriffe.erklaerung: Black stripes from the eye to the mouth.
Grassland with scattered trees in warm regions.
The time in which an animal carries its young in its belly.
A list that shows how strongly animal and plant species are threatened.

gewusst: Cheetahs cannot roar like lions, but they purr like house cats and make chirping sounds.
A cheetah accelerates faster than many sports cars.
The German name Gepard probably comes from an Italian word for “spotted pard”.

teile.einleitung: Genetic diversity means that the animals or plants of a species differ in their genetic make-up. That is why not every fox looks exactly the same and not every cow is equally resistant. These differences are like a toolbox with which a species can adapt to new conditions.
wichtigste: Genetic diversity is the variety of genetic make-up within a species.
Besides the diversity of species and of habitats, it is a part of biodiversity.
Genetic diversity increases the ability to adapt to changes in the environment.
That is why it is very important for the protection of species.
Small, isolated populations often lose genetic diversity.
Inbreeding can favour illnesses and weaknesses.
Old breeds of farm animals and plant varieties also preserve genetic diversity.

abschnitte.text: Every living thing has **genes** in its cells, which act like a blueprint. Within a species there are slightly different versions of many genes. That is why people have different eye colours, and cats have different coat patterns. The more such versions there are in a species, the greater its genetic diversity. It is one of three levels of **biodiversity**, alongside the diversity of species and of habitats.

The environment is constantly changing, for example through the climate, new diseases or new enemies. If the animals of a species are different, some may have exactly the characteristics that help in the new situation. These animals are more likely to survive and pass on their genes. In this way genetic diversity increases the **adaptability** of a species. If, on the other hand, all the animals are almost the same, a single disease can threaten a whole population.

When only a few animals of a species are left, close relatives often mate. This is called **inbreeding**. Hereditary diseases can then occur more often, and the animals sometimes become weaker or less fertile. A well-known example is the cheetah, whose genetic diversity is very low. It is suspected that its ancestors were once, long ago, reduced to very few animals.

The Alpine ibex was wiped out in Switzerland in the 19th century. From 1906, animals from Italy were reintroduced, all of which came from one small remnant population. Today many thousands of ibex live in the Swiss Alps again, but their genetic diversity is low. Experts therefore take care to connect populations with each other. The bearded vulture, too, is bred and released in such a way that as much diversity as possible is preserved.

Zoos keep **studbooks** so that related animals do not always have young together. For plants, seed banks store the seeds of many varieties, for example the large seed vault on Svalbard in Norway. In Switzerland, the foundation **ProSpecieRara** has worked since 1982 for old breeds of farm animals and plant varieties. Wildlife bridges over motorways help animals to move between areas and to mix. In this way genetic diversity is preserved in the future too.

begriffe.erklaerung: A section of the genetic material that helps to determine a particular characteristic.
The diversity of life: species, habitats and genetic make-up.
Reproduction between closely related animals.
The ability to cope with new environmental conditions.

gewusst: All the ibex in Switzerland descend from only a few dozen animals from an Italian mountain valley.
In Ireland in the 19th century, a fungal disease led to a great famine, partly because almost everywhere the same variety of potato was grown.
Cheetahs are so similar genetically that in experiments skin from an unrelated animal could be transplanted onto them without being rejected.

teile.einleitung: An ischial callosity is a hardened, hairless patch of skin on the bottom of some monkeys, for example baboons. It works like a built-in seat cushion. With it, the animals can sit for hours on hard branches or rocks and even sleep sitting up.
wichtigste: An ischial callosity is a hardened, hairless patch of skin on the bottom.
In German it is called a Gesässschwiele or Sitzschwiele.
Baboons, macaques, guenons and gibbons have such callosities.
The callosities lie over the sitting bones of the pelvis.
They allow the monkeys to sit comfortably on branches and rocks.
Many of these monkeys sleep sitting up.
The red swelling in female baboons is something different from the callosity.

abschnitte.text: An **ischial callosity** is a pad of thickened, hardened skin on the rear end. No hair grows there. The skin is very firm, similar to the hard skin on the soles of our feet. It lies exactly over the **sitting bones**, which are the bones of the pelvis that you sit on. Experts also call them sitting callosities.

Ischial callosities are found above all in the **Old World monkeys** of Africa and Asia. They include baboons, macaques such as the rhesus monkey, guenons and langurs. Gibbons, the small apes, also have sitting callosities. In great apes such as gorillas or orang-utans they are mostly missing. The monkeys of South and Central America have no ischial callosities.

Many monkeys spend a great deal of time sitting, while eating, resting and grooming. The callosities cushion the bottom against hard surfaces. They are particularly practical for **sleeping**: baboons and macaques often sleep sitting on branches or rock ledges. This way they are better protected at night from predators such as leopards. The hard skin prevents them from getting sore from sitting.

In female baboons you sometimes see a strongly swollen, bright red bottom. This is not the callosity but a **sexual swelling**. It shows the males that the female is fertile at that moment. Afterwards the swelling goes down again. In the mandrill, too, the bottom is strikingly colourful, especially in the males.

abschnitte.titel: Easy to watch in the zoo
abschnitte.text: In many zoos, also in Switzerland, you can watch baboons or macaques sitting. The callosities are easy to recognise as grey or dark bare patches. They grow with the animal and are already present in young animals. For researchers they are also a feature for telling groups of monkeys apart. A small part of the body thus shows how well animals are adapted to their way of life.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thickened, hard patch of skin that forms through pressure or friction.
Bony projections of the pelvis that you sit on.
Monkeys that live in Africa and Asia.
A red swelling on the bottom that shows fertility in some female monkeys.

gewusst: Some baboons sleep every night sitting on rocky cliffs, with the callosities serving as cushions.
Humans, too, get calluses, for example on the fingers from playing the guitar.
In hamadryas baboons the skin around the callosities is often bright red.

teile.einleitung: Royal jelly, in French gelée royale, is a special food secretion that honeybees make. The workers use it to feed above all the larvae from which a new queen is to develop. This “royal food” turns an ordinary larva into a large, long-lived queen bee.
wichtigste: Royal jelly is a food secretion of honeybees.
Young workers produce it in glands in the head.
A future queen gets particularly much royal jelly, throughout her whole larval life.
Other larvae receive the food secretion only in the first days.
The special food makes sure that a larva becomes a queen.
Royal jelly is whitish, creamy and tastes slightly sour.
People sell it as a food supplement, but a healing effect has not been proved.

abschnitte.text: **Gelée royale** is French and means “royal jelly”. It is a white to yellowish, creamy mass. It consists to a large part of water, together with proteins, sugar, fats and vitamins. The bees do not make it from flowers as they do honey, but produce it themselves in their bodies.

Royal jelly is produced by young workers who are about five to fifteen days old. They are called **nurse bees**. They have special food glands in their heads. So that they can produce the secretion, they eat a lot of pollen. Later, when they are older, these glands shrink, and the bees take on other jobs in the hive.

All bee larvae get some royal jelly in the first days. After that, the larvae of workers receive simpler food with honey and pollen. A larva in a particularly large **queen cell**, on the other hand, gets plenty of royal jelly throughout its whole larval life. It develops into a queen, who is larger than the workers and can lay eggs. A queen needs only about 16 days from egg to emergence, a worker about 21 days.

abschnitte.titel: Living long thanks to special food
abschnitte.text: The adult queen, too, is still fed with royal jelly by the workers. She can live for several years. A worker, by contrast, often lives only a few weeks in summer. In spring and summer a queen lays up to about 2,000 eggs a day. For this she needs a great deal of energy from the nourishing food secretion.

Beekeepers can obtain royal jelly from queen cells, but only in small amounts and with a lot of work. It is sold as a **food supplement** or in cosmetics. It is often claimed that it makes you healthy or young. Such an effect in humans has not been scientifically proved, however. People with allergies can even react badly to it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A young worker bee that feeds and cares for the larvae.
A particularly large honeycomb cell in which a new queen grows up.
The maggot-like young form of the bee that hatches from the egg.
A gland in the head of the bee that produces royal jelly.

gewusst: Whether a larva becomes a queen or a worker depends not on the genes but mainly on the food.
If a colony suddenly has no queen any more, the bees can raise a new queen from a young worker larva.
A queen bee can live much longer than a worker, although both hatch from the same kind of egg.

teile.einleitung: Antlers are the head decoration of deer. Unlike horns, they consist of bone and are shed and regrown every year. While they are growing, they are soft and covered with a velvety skin, the velvet.
wichtigste: Antlers consist of bone and grow from the frontal bone of deer.
They are shed every year and grow again.
The growing antlers are covered with velvet, a skin with a good blood supply.
When the antlers are finished, the stag rubs off the velvet, which is called fraying.
Usually only the males carry antlers.
In reindeer both sexes carry antlers.
The horns of cows, chamois or ibex are something different from antlers.

abschnitte.text: **Antlers** are a structure of bone that grows on the head of deer. They sit on two short bony stumps, the **pedicles**. The individual branches are called beams, and their tips are called points. A stag with twelve points is therefore called a twelve-pointer. The deer family includes, for example, the red deer, roe deer, elk and reindeer.

A new set of antlers grows very fast, much faster than other bones. During growth it is soft and covered with skin, the **velvet**. The velvet is threaded with many blood vessels and brings nutrients to the growing bone. When the antlers are finished, the velvet dies. The stag then rubs it off on trees and bushes, which is called **fraying**.

After the mating season, the antlers detach from the pedicle and fall off. In the red deer this happens around late winter, in the roe deer already in autumn or early winter. Straight afterwards a new set of antlers begins to grow. In reindeer, too, the antlers are shed every year and grow anew. The shed beams are called cast antlers, and they are sometimes found in the woods.

Antlers are important above all for the **rut**, the mating season. With them the males show how strong and healthy they are. When two equally strong stags meet, they fight by locking their antlers against each other. Large antlers impress rivals and females. In reindeer the females also use their antlers, for example to defend feeding places in winter.

Antlers are not the same as horns. **Horns** consist of a bony core with a sheath of horn, similar to our fingernails. They are not shed but keep growing throughout life. Horns are carried by cows, goats, chamois and ibex, for example. In Switzerland, red deer and roe deer live with antlers, while chamois and ibex, by contrast, have horns.

begriffe.erklaerung: The velvety skin with a good blood supply that covers growing antlers.
Rubbing off the dead velvet on trees and bushes.
A bony stump on the skull on which the antlers sit.
The mating season of deer.

gewusst: Antlers are among the fastest growing tissues in the whole animal kingdom.
The elk has the largest antlers of all deer living today, with broad palms.
Shed antlers are often gnawed by mice and other animals, because they contain valuable minerals.

teile.einleitung: The common house mosquito is one of the most frequent species of mosquito in Switzerland. If you hear a fine buzzing at your ear on a summer night, it is often this one. Only the females bite, because they need blood so that their eggs can ripen.
wichtigste: The common house mosquito is called Culex pipiens in science.
It is one of the most frequent species of mosquito in Switzerland.
Only the females bite and suck blood.
The males feed on plant juices and nectar.
Their larvae live in standing water, for example in rain barrels.
The mosquito is active mainly at dusk and at night.
Mated females spend the winter in cellars and sheds.

abschnitte.text: The common house mosquito is about 5 to 7 millimetres long and brownish in colour. It has long, thin legs and two narrow wings. The female has a long **proboscis** with which she pierces the skin. The males can be recognised by their bushy antennae. The typical buzzing arises because the mosquito beats its wings several hundred times a second.

Only the females suck blood, because they need the protein in the blood for the development of their eggs. They find their victims mainly by the **carbon dioxide** that we breathe out, by body warmth and by smells. The common house mosquito particularly likes to bite birds, but also humans. When biting, she releases saliva into the wound so that the blood does not clot. Our body reacts to this saliva, which is why it itches and a swelling forms.

The female lays her eggs as a small, floating **egg raft** on standing water. From these hatch larvae that hang head down at the surface of the water and take in air through a breathing tube. After that follows a pupal stage, also in the water. In warm weather the whole development takes only about two to three weeks. Even a rain barrel, a watering can or a forgotten flowerpot saucer is enough as a nursery.

The common house mosquito occurs almost everywhere in Switzerland, especially in built-up areas. It is on the move at dusk and at night and likes to fly through open windows into bedrooms. In autumn the mated females look for frost-free places such as cellars, garages or caves. There they spend the winter in a kind of resting state. In spring they then begin laying eggs.

To protect yourself, **mosquito screens** on windows and long clothing in the evening help. You should cover rain barrels and regularly empty standing water in the garden. In some countries the common house mosquito can transmit disease agents such as the West Nile virus. In Switzerland such cases have so far been very rare. For nature, mosquitoes and their larvae are important food, for example for bats, swallows, fish and dragonflies.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long, fine mouthpart with which the mosquito bites and sucks.
The young form of the mosquito, which lives in the water.
Many mosquito eggs stuck together that float on the water.
A gas that humans and animals breathe out and that attracts mosquitoes.

gewusst: When sucking blood, a mosquito can take in more than its own body weight in blood.
Male mosquitoes never bite, because their proboscis is not even built for it.
For some years now the introduced Asian tiger mosquito has also been spreading in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Chamois Coloured goat, in German Gämsfarbige Gebirgsziege, is a Swiss goat breed and the most common goat breed in the country. It is brown like a chamois and has a black stripe on its back. As a hardy dairy goat, it is as much at home in the mountains as in the lowlands.
wichtigste: The Chamois Coloured goat is a breed of domestic goat from Switzerland.
It is the most common goat breed in Switzerland.
Its coat is brown with a black stripe on the back.
The belly and legs are also coloured black.
It is kept mainly for its milk.
It is hardy, undemanding and well adapted to life in the mountains.
In North America, a related breed is called the Oberhasli.

abschnitte.text: The Chamois Coloured goat has a short, reddish brown to chestnut coat. A black **dorsal stripe** runs over the back, as in many wild animals. The belly and lower legs are black, so it looks as if it were wearing black boots. It also has black stripes on the face. This colouring is reminiscent of the wild **chamois**, hence the name.

The breed comes from the Swiss Alps, above all from Graubünden and the Bernese Oberland. Today it is bred throughout Switzerland. It is the largest **goat breed** in the country by number. It is also kept in other countries, for example in Germany, Austria and the USA.

The Chamois Coloured goat is above all a **dairy goat**. A good doe gives several hundred litres of milk a year. From goat's milk people make cheese, yoghurt and fresh cheese, for example the popular goat's fresh cheese. In part the meat of the young animals, the kids, is also eaten. Goats also help to keep steep Alpine pastures open, because they eat bushes and shrubs.

The breed is adapted to the rough mountain climate. It climbs surely in steep terrain and manages on sparse food. Goats eat grass, herbs, leaves and twigs. They are curious and intelligent animals that live in a **herd**. Some animals carry horns, others are naturally hornless.

In Switzerland there are several native goat breeds, for example the Saanen goat, the Toggenburg goat and the Valais Blackneck goat. The Chamois Coloured goat is the most common among them. Breeding is supported by the **Swiss Goat Breeders' Association**. Breeders pay attention to health, milk yield and the typical colour. The female is called a doe, the male a buck and the young a kid.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dark stripe that runs down the middle of the back.
A group of domestic animals of one species with shared features.
The Swiss word for a young kid.
A goat that is kept mainly for its milk.

gewusst: Goats were among the first animals that humans turned into domestic animals, about 10,000 years ago.
Goats can pluck individual leaves very skilfully with their lips.
In North America the Chamois Coloured goat is known under the name Oberhasli, after a region in the Bernese Oberland.

teile.einleitung: The common earwig is a brown insect with a striking pair of pincers at its rear end. Despite its name, it does not crawl into ears, which is only an old superstition. It is even a useful helper in the garden and a particularly caring mother.
wichtigste: The common earwig is called Forficula auricularia in science.
On its abdomen it carries pincers, which are strongly curved in the male and straighter in the female.
It eats plant and animal food, and particularly likes aphids.
By day it hides in dark crevices under stones or bark.
It can fly, but does so rather rarely.
The female lays her eggs in a burrow in the ground and tends them.
Unusual for insects: the mother also looks after the young larvae.

abschnitte.text: The common earwig is about 1 to 1.6 centimetres long and reddish brown. Its body is flat and elongated, so it fits into narrow cracks. At the rear end sit **pincers**, which consist of two modified appendages. In the male they are strong and strongly curved, in the female straighter. Under the short wing cases lie large, cleverly folded membranous wings.

abschnitte.titel: Way of life and hiding places
abschnitte.text: Earwigs are **nocturnal**. By day they like to hide in dark, damp crevices under stones, under bark or in flowers. Often many animals sit close together. Although they can fly, they do so rather rarely. Mostly they scurry about nimbly on their six legs.

The earwig is an **omnivore** and eats plant and animal food. It particularly likes to eat aphids, mites and insect eggs. That is why many gardeners are pleased to have earwigs, especially on fruit trees. Sometimes, however, it also nibbles at flowers, soft fruit or young leaves. With an upturned flowerpot full of wood wool or straw, a so-called **earwig hotel**, you can lure it into the garden.

In autumn or winter the female digs a small burrow in the ground and lays her eggs there. She stays with the eggs and cleans them again and again. In this way she protects them above all from mould and fungi. Even after hatching, the mother still looks after the young larvae and sometimes brings them food. This **brood care** is unusual in insects.

If an earwig feels threatened, it raises its pincers in a threatening way. If it pinches a finger with them, it is usually only a slight nip and harmless. In addition it can defend itself with a foul-smelling **secretion**. The name probably comes from the old belief that the animal crawls into the ears of sleeping people. That is not true, however, earwigs just like narrow, dark hiding places.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two curved appendages on the abdomen for threatening, defending and folding the wings.
When parents protect and look after their eggs or young.
A liquid that an animal releases from glands.
An upturned flowerpot filled with straw as a shelter for earwigs.

gewusst: Earwigs also use their pincers to fold their large hind wings back together after a flight.
The hind wings of the earwig are folded so cleverly that engineers study them as a model for foldable technology.
In German, an “Ohrwurm”, like an “earworm” in English, is also a song that you cannot get out of your head.

teile.einleitung: Orthopterans, in German Geradflügler, is another name for the grasshoppers and their relatives, a large order of insects. They include grasshoppers, crickets and bush crickets. Many of them can jump far and chirp with their legs or wings.
wichtigste: Grasshoppers belong to the insect order of the orthopterans.
The scientific name is Orthoptera, which means “straight wings”.
Worldwide there are over 25,000 species.
A distinction is made between long-horned and short-horned grasshoppers.
Most have strong jumping legs.
Many species produce sounds by rubbing parts of the body together.
About 100 species of grasshopper live in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The **orthopterans** are an order of insects to which all grasshoppers belong. The German name Geradflügler, “straight-winged”, comes from the narrow, straight front wings that lie over the body at rest. Underneath, the broader hind wings are folded like a fan. Typical, too, are the long, strong hind legs with which the animals jump. Worldwide, over 25,000 species are known.

The **long-horned grasshoppers** have antennae that are often longer than their body. They include bush crickets such as the great green bush cricket, and the crickets. The **short-horned grasshoppers** have short, strong antennae. They include the field grasshoppers that you see jumping on meadows in summer. The dreaded locusts are also short-horned grasshoppers.

Many orthopterans make music, which is called **stridulation**. Field grasshoppers rub their hind legs against their wings, while crickets and bush crickets rub their wings against each other. Mostly the males sing, to attract females. Every species has its own song, and experts recognise the species by their singing. The ears of bush crickets sit on the front legs and those of field grasshoppers on the abdomen.

Orthopterans go through an **incomplete metamorphosis**. A larva hatches from the egg that already looks similar to the adult animals but does not yet have finished wings. It moults several times and grows bigger each time. After the last moult it is adult and can fly. There is no pupal stage as in a butterfly.

About 100 species of grasshopper live in Switzerland, from crickets on the Central Plateau to mountain species on the Alpine pastures. Well-known species are the field cricket, the great green bush cricket and the mole cricket, which digs in the ground with its shovel-like legs. Many species need flower-rich meadows that are not mown too often. Because such meadows have become rarer, some species are on the Red List. Grasshoppers are important food for birds, lizards and many other animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group in the classification of living things, for example beetles or butterflies.
Producing sounds by rubbing parts of the body together.
Development without a pupa, in which the larvae resemble the adults.
A long sense organ on the head of insects.

gewusst: Some locusts form huge swarms of billions of animals that eat whole fields bare.
In crickets you can roughly estimate the temperature from the speed of the chirping, because in warmth they chirp faster.
In many countries grasshoppers are eaten, and they contain a lot of protein.
